chapters.title: The Computational Thinker
chapters.learn:
A computational thinker solves big problems the way a builder makes a robot: one small piece at a time.

Four super-skills

Decomposition – break a problem into small parts.
Pattern recognition – spot what repeats.
Abstraction – keep what matters, ignore the rest.
Algorithms – write clear steps anyone can follow.

Simple or difficult?

A simple problem has clear steps and one answer. A difficult problem has many choices, feelings or surprises, so we must break it down first.

questions.q: Which object is needed to balance the last scale?
questions.hint: Use the second scale to compare a truck with cars.
s: The second scale shows 2 cars and 1 truck weigh the same as 2 trucks. Remove 1 truck from each side: 1 truck = 2 cars.
On the last scale, 1 car + 1 truck = 1 + 2 = 3 cars. The left side already has 3 cars’ worth without the bus.
The right side already has 3 cars, so the bus on the left must be matched by a bus on the right. Answer: Bus.

questions.q: Is each everyday problem Simple or Difficult?
items: Helping a friend who is feeling upset or worried
Organizing our school bag before leaving for school
Deciding what to do after missing the train
Following a recipe to prepare a sandwich
Finding a safe way home during heavy rain
questions.hint: Simple = clear steps. Difficult = many choices or feelings.
s: Simple problems have clear steps and one result: packing a bag and following a recipe.
Difficult problems involve feelings, choices or changing situations: helping a friend, missing the train, and a rainy journey home.

questions.q: Each 👧 = 2 students (half = 1). X = half of (Strawberry + Banana). Y = Pear + Mango. Which fruit equals the difference between X and Y?
questions.hint: First turn the symbols into numbers of students.
s: Full symbol = 2 students, half = 1. Strawberry 12, Banana 8, Pear 9, Mango 13.
Difference = 22 − 10 = 12. Strawberry has 6 symbols = 12 students.

questions.q: Akash: minute hand at 12, hour hand 150° clockwise from it. Chirag: hour hand at 5, minute hand 210° clockwise from it. Which is correct?
questions.hint: Each number on a clock is 30° apart.
s: 150° ÷ 30° = 5 steps from 12, so Akash’s hour hand is at 5. The time is 5:00.
210° ÷ 30° = 7 steps from 5, which lands on 12. The minute hand is at 12, the hour hand at 5: also 5:00.
Both came at exactly 5:00. Answer: same time.

questions.q: The printer will not print. Tap the steps in the correct order.
items: Check the printer has paper and ink. Look for a jam or error.
Restart the printer and computer, then print a test page.
Open the Print box and choose the right printer.
Check the USB cable is firmly connected at both ends.
Check the printer is plugged in and switched on.
questions.hint: Start with the easiest, most basic check.
s: Start with power: is it plugged in and on?
Next the cable, then the software choice in the Print box.
Then paper, ink and jams. Restart last, if nothing else worked.
questions.review: Order inferred – please confirm with the academic team.

chapters.title: The Power of Abstract Thinking
chapters.learn:
Abstraction means keeping the important details and ignoring the rest. A map does not show every leaf, only roads and landmarks.

Look for what matters

Numbers in a table, neighbours in a grid, or the shape of an edge: find the rule, then use it again and again.

Predict with patterns

If something grows by the same amount each time, you can predict what comes next.

questions.q: Shoot ❌ one item in each box. It disappears along with identical items in neighbouring boxes. Most items you can remove after 3 shots?
questions.hint: The middle box touches both outer boxes. Which shape is in all three?
s: Left shot: red diamond removes 2 (left and middle).
Middle shot: yellow triangle removes 3 (one in each box).
Right shot: pink octagon removes 2 (middle and right). Total: 2 + 3 + 2 = 7.

questions.q: How many blocks touch at least one smaller and one larger number?
questions.vis:
235 – 410 – 381
167 – 453 – 579
284 – 831 – 531
(blocks joined by lines in a 3×3 grid)
questions.hint: Check each block’s linked neighbours only.
s: Count only blocks joined by a line.
235 (167 and 410), 410 (235 and 453), 453 (410 and 579) and 284 (167 and 831) each have a smaller and a larger neighbour.
That makes 4 blocks.

questions.q: Sandwiches sold in weeks 1–5: 100, 125, 150, 175, 200. How many in week 6?
questions.hint: How much does it grow each week?
s: Look at the gaps: 125 − 100 = 25, 150 − 125 = 25 and so on.
Sales grow by 25 every week.

questions.q: A rabbit starts at −8 on this line: −12, −10, ⬜, −4, ⬜, 0 … 6, 8, … 14. It jumps to the 9th point right, then the 7th point left. Add the values of all places it landed, including the start.
questions.review: Solution drafted by AI – needs approval.
s: From −8, 9 points right: −8 + 18 = 10.
From 10, 7 points left: 10 − 14 = −4.
